summary: A royal wedding parable portrays invited guests refusing, abusing messengers, and facing judgment; replacement guests fill the hall, but one guest found without wedding clothing shows that attendance itself is not enough. Opposing groups then pose traps about imperial tax, resurrection, and the greatest command. Jesus asks for Caesar's image while insisting on what belongs to God, corrects Sadducees through Torah's living God, joins love of God and neighbor, and ends by asking how David's son can also be David's Lord.
whyItMatters: The chapter answers attempts to reduce allegiance to a slogan, faction, or puzzle. Human beings bear more than Caesar's image; resurrection exceeds present social arrangements; the Law and Prophets hang on integrated love; and Messiah cannot be contained inside a merely dynastic expectation.

context.author: Anonymous narrator arranging Jerusalem controversy stories
context.audience: Greek-speaking readers, probably Jewish and Gentile, here following arguments over empire, resurrection debate, Torah interpretation, and messianic identity
context.date: After AD 70 on most current dating, often the 80s or 90s; earlier dates are defended
context.setting: Jerusalem temple precincts in the final public disputes
context.literaryForm: Judgment parable followed by four public controversy exchanges

outline.heading: Wedding invitation refused and the unready guest
outline.note: Invited guests refuse a king's wedding feast and kill his servants; strangers fill it; a man without wedding clothing is thrown out

outline.heading: Caesar's coin and God's claim
outline.note: Asked about taxes to Caesar, Jesus asks for the tax coin and whose image it bears; give Caesar and God their own

outline.heading: Sadducees, marriage, and resurrection
outline.note: Sadducees pose seven brothers and one widow; Jesus says none marry in the resurrection; God is 'not the God of the dead'

outline.heading: Love of God and neighbor
outline.note: A lawyer asks the greatest commandment; Jesus answers 'love the Lord your God', then your neighbor as yourself

outline.heading: David's son and David's Lord
outline.note: Jesus asks whose son the Christ is; they say 'Of David'; how then does David call him Lord? No one answers

keyVerses.text: They said to him, “Caesar’s.” Then he said to them, “Give therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”
keyVerses.why: The answer recognizes a limited civic claim while placing it inside God's unlimited claim.

keyVerses.text: Jesus said to him, “‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.’
keyVerses.why: Deuteronomy's command directs the whole person toward God rather than dividing life into religious fragments.

keyVerses.text: A second likewise is this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’
keyVerses.why: Leviticus's neighbor command is made inseparable from love of God and supports the whole scriptural teaching.

questions.question: Why is the wedding parable so violent?
questions.answer: Royal wedding parables operate at an exaggerated scale of allegiance and judgment. Matthew also adapts the scene to evoke rejection of messengers and a city's destruction. It should not be read as a manual for human rulers or as ethnic revenge; it is an apocalyptic warning that refusing the king's invitation and abusing emissaries has consequences.

questions.question: Why punish someone pulled in from the roads for lacking wedding clothes?
questions.answer: The second scene shifts from receiving an invitation to responding appropriately. The man is speechless when addressed as ‘friend,’ suggesting refusal rather than inability in the parable's symbolic world. Matthew warns that inclusion is gracious but not empty of transformation. The image should not be used to shame literal poverty or clothing.

questions.question: What trap is hidden in the tax question?
questions.answer: On the usual reading, endorsing the Roman head tax risks sounding loyal to occupation; rejecting it risks a charge of rebellion. The Pharisees send their disciples with the Herodians to set the trap (22:15-16). Jesus requests the incriminating coin from them and reframes the issue around ownership and allegiance.

questions.question: Does ‘render to Caesar’ give government everything it asks?
questions.answer: Apodidōmi means give back what is due. Caesar's image is on the coin, but humans bear God's image and everything belongs ultimately to God. Jesus neither announces tax revolt nor grants empire unlimited sacred authority. The second clause relativizes the first and requires discernment whenever Caesar claims what belongs to God.

questions.question: What is the Sadducees' seven-husband puzzle?
questions.answer: It applies levirate marriage, which preserved a dead brother's line through his widow, to ridicule resurrection. Sadducees denied the resurrection, which Pharisees affirmed (Acts 23:8). Jesus says they project present arrangements into God's transformed future and underestimate both Scripture and divine power.

questions.question: How does ‘I am the God of Abraham’ argue for resurrection?
questions.answer: Jesus quotes Exodus (3:6), from the books of Moses the Sadducees have just cited (22:24), and presses the present covenant formula: God is not God of dead people but of living. The argument is relational — God's faithful bond with the patriarchs is not dissolved by death — rather than a dictionary proof from verb tense alone.

questions.question: Do heart, soul, and mind describe three separable human parts?
questions.answer: The accumulated terms express total-person love, not an anatomy chart. Matthew's wording of Deuteronomy 6:5 has dianoia, ‘mind,’ where the hosted Deuteronomy has ‘might,’ emphasizing understanding alongside heart and soul/life. Repetition means no dimension of allegiance is withheld.

questions.question: Why ask whether the Messiah is David's son if Matthew calls Jesus Son of David?
questions.answer: Jesus does not deny Davidic descent; he uses Psalm 110 to show the title is insufficient by itself. David addresses the Messiah as ‘my Lord,’ so the descendant also exceeds the ancestor. The question expands messianic identity beyond genealogy toward exalted lordship.

glossary.def: Partisans of the Herod family, named beside the Pharisees' disciples in 22:16.
A Jewish movement tied to the high priest (Acts 5:17) and to men of high rank (Josephus, Antiquities 18.1.4) that rejected resurrection and differed sharply from Pharisees (Acts 23:8).
A Torah practice through which a brother could preserve the name and line of a deceased man (Deuteronomy 25:5-6) through his widow.
